title: AC Running but Not Cooling the House? Causes
h1: Why Is My AC Running but Not Cooling the House?
description: If your AC runs but the house stays warm, check the filter, thermostat, outdoor unit and ducts. Here are the common causes and when to call a technician.
quick_answer: An AC that runs without cooling the house usually has a dirty filter, a frozen or dirty coil, an outdoor unit that is not running, low refrigerant, leaking ducts or a system that cannot keep up with the heat. Check the filter, thermostat and outdoor unit first, then call for service if the air is still not cool.
body:
You hear the system running, air is moving, but the house stays warm. That's one of the most common summer calls we get. A few causes are easy to check yourself. The rest point to specific repairs a technician can track down.

Is the air coming out of the vents cool?

Hold your hand up to a supply register after the system has run for 15 minutes or so. This tells you which direction to look.

  • The air feels warm or room temperature. The system isn't cooling the air. Look at the thermostat, filter, outdoor unit, coils and refrigerant.
  • The air feels cool, but the house won't cool down. The system may be cooling but losing that cool air to leaky ducts, a hot attic or poor insulation, or it may be too small for the heat load.

What can you check first?

  1. Thermostat. Set to Cool, fan on Auto, setpoint a few degrees below room temperature.
  2. Filter. A dirty filter is one of the most common causes of poor cooling. Replace it.
  3. Outdoor unit. Go outside while the system is calling for cooling. The fan should spin and you should hear the compressor. If it's silent, check the breaker and the outdoor disconnect.
  4. Registers and returns. Open closed registers and move furniture away from return grilles.
  5. Ice. Look at the copper lines near the outdoor unit and at the indoor unit. If you see frost or ice, turn cooling off and let it thaw.

What causes warm air when the system is running?

The outdoor unit isn't running

If only the indoor blower is on, you're just moving warm air around. A tripped breaker, failed capacitor, bad contactor or a safety switch can stop the outdoor unit. If a breaker trips again after one reset, leave it off. Capacitors and contactors carry high voltage and need a technician.

A frozen indoor coil

Low airflow or low refrigerant can make the indoor coil freeze. Once it's iced over, air can't pass through it and cooling stops. Thaw it with cooling off, replace the filter and try again. If it refreezes, call for service.

A dirty outdoor coil

Dust, leaves and plant debris on the outdoor coil trap heat in the system. Coastal homes also deal with salt residue and corrosion. With the power off, you can rinse loose debris from the outside with a gentle hose stream. Deeper cleaning is part of a tune-up.

Low refrigerant

Refrigerant doesn't get used up, so low refrigerant means there's a leak. Signs include ice on the lines, hissing and cooling that has faded over time. The leak should be found and repaired before the system is recharged.

What if the air is cool but the house stays warm?

Leaky or disconnected ducts

In many Southern California homes the ducts run through the attic, which can get extremely hot in summer. A disconnected duct, a crushed flex run or leaky joints can dump cool air into the attic before it reaches your rooms. One or two rooms that never cool off is a classic sign.

A hot attic and thin insulation

If attic insulation is thin, compressed or damaged by pests, heat pours down through the ceiling all afternoon. The AC runs and runs but can't keep up. Upstairs rooms in two-story homes feel it the most.

A system that's too small or too old

An undersized system may keep up on a mild day and fall behind on a hot one. An aging system that has lost efficiency can do the same. On the hottest inland afternoons, even a healthy system may run nonstop and sit a degree or two above the setpoint, but it should catch up as the evening cools.

When should you call for service?

Call a technician if the simple checks don't help or if you notice:

  • Ice that comes back after thawing.
  • A breaker that trips repeatedly.
  • Grinding, buzzing, clicking or hissing from the outdoor unit.
  • A burning smell.
  • Water around the indoor unit.

Our technicians check the full system, including refrigerant, electrical parts, coils, airflow and ducts, so the fix targets the real cause. Learn more about our air conditioning repair service. If the problem is in the ducts, our duct sealing and repair service covers that too.
faqs: Why is my AC running but the house is not getting cooler?

If the vent air is warm, the system is not cooling, often from a dirty filter, frozen coil, outdoor unit problem or low refrigerant. If the vent air is cool but the house stays warm, look at leaky attic ducts, poor insulation or a system too small for the home.
How long should it take for my AC to cool the house?

It depends on the house, the outdoor temperature and the system size. A properly working system should make steady progress. If the temperature barely moves after a few hours on a normal day, something needs attention.
Can a dirty filter stop my AC from cooling?
Yes. A clogged filter restricts airflow, which reduces cooling and can cause the indoor coil to freeze. Replacing the filter is the first thing to try.
Is it bad to run my AC if it is not cooling?
Running it can make a frozen coil worse or strain the compressor. Turn cooling off after your quick checks and have it looked at if it still is not cooling.
Why Is My AC Blowing Warm Air? The Easy Checks First?

An AC usually blows warm air because of a thermostat set to fan or heat, a dirty filter, a tripped breaker or switch at the outdoor unit, a dirty outdoor coil, low refrigerant or a failed capacitor. Check the thermostat, filter and breakers first. If the air is still warm, shut it off and have it diagnosed.
